\chapter{The Word That Was Deferred}
\label{ch:ur-word-that-was-deferred}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I do not understand, put \ur{نہیں} in front of any verb this book has taught, turn any statement into a yes-or-no question with \ur{کیا} at the front, and refuse two things at once with \ur{نہ} … \ur{نہ}.}

The sentence chapter one explicitly deferred -- \ur{میں} \ur{نہیں} \ur{سمجھتا} -- is said at last, and the question \ur{جی} \ur{ہاں} and \ur{نہیں} were taught to answer eighteen chapters ago can finally be asked.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā]{\ur{میں} \ur{نہیں} \ur{سمجھتا} — the sentence chapter one promised}

\label{lesson:UR-C19-nahin-verb}



\begin{quote}
Chapter one taught \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} and said, in as many words, that its second job — \emph{not}, inside a sentence — would matter once the book had verbs. Fourteen verbs later, here it is.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the wellbeing reply — \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{نہیں} in front of the verb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{نہیں} \ur{سمجھتا}} — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} — \textbf{I do not understand} (man speaking)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{نہیں} \ur{سمجھتی}} — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtī} — the same, a woman speaking
\end{quote}

Take the affirmative frame chapter seven built, \emph{maiṅ samajhtā hūṅ}, and put \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} in front of the verb. Nothing else moves, and one thing is allowed to disappear: with \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} in the sentence, the closing \textbf{\ur{ہوں}} is usually dropped in speech. Both \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} and \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā hūṅ} are correct; the shorter one is what people say.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the negator stands}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\emph{maiṅ samajhtā hūṅ} & I understand \\
\emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} & I do not understand \\
\emph{maiṅ nahīṅ jāntā} & I do not know \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ur{نہیں}} goes \textbf{before} the verb, not after it. That is the opposite of Bengali and the same as English, which puts \emph{not} before \emph{understand} as well. The agreement stays on the verb and the negator never changes shape.

The three letters of \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} are all yours: \textbf{\ur{ن}}, \textbf{\ur{ہ}}, \textbf{\ur{ی}}, and the dotless \textbf{\ur{ں}} that hums at the end. The verb beside it is not — three of its letters are still ahead of you in the script ladder — so it is printed here in the word this lesson owns and left in romanization everywhere else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the affirmative first — \emph{maiṅ samajhtā hūṅ}
  \item \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}
  \item \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ jāntā} — I do not know
  \item \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ bōltā} — I do not speak
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} stand in relation to the verb? (\textbf{Before it}.) What happens to \textbf{\ur{ہوں}} when the negator arrives? (\textbf{It is usually dropped}, and keeping it is not wrong.) And what still marks who is speaking? (\textbf{The verb ending} — \emph{-tā} or \emph{-tī}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?]{\ur{کیا} \ur{آپ} \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہیں؟} — the question that could not be asked}

\label{lesson:UR-C19-kya-polar}



\begin{quote}
\emph{jī hāṅ} and \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} were the first two words this book taught, and they answer a question. Eighteen chapters have gone by without the book being able to ask it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the item before this one — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کیا} at the front}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کیا} \ur{آپ} \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہیں؟}} — \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?} — \textbf{are you well?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کیا} \ur{یہ} \ur{پانی} \ur{ہے؟}} — \emph{kyā yih pānī hai?} — \textbf{is this water?}
\end{quote}

Chapter three taught \textbf{\ur{کیا}} as \emph{what}. Put it at the \textbf{front} of a statement and it stops meaning \emph{what} altogether: it marks the whole sentence as a yes-or-no question, and nothing else in the sentence moves.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one word, two jobs, told apart by position}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where \ur{کیا} stands} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
in the middle & \textbf{what} \\
at the front & \textbf{(yes-or-no)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Position is the whole difference. English cannot do this: it has to move the verb in front of the subject, \emph{you are} becoming \emph{are you}. Urdu adds one word at the edge and leaves the sentence alone. In speech the fronted \textbf{\ur{کیا}} is often left out and the rise of the voice carries it by itself.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?} — then answer it \emph{jī hāṅ} or \emph{nahīṅ}
  \item \emph{kyā yih pānī hai?}
  \item the same question without the word, on the voice alone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tells you whether \textbf{\ur{کیا}} means \emph{what} or marks a yes-or-no question? (\textbf{Where it stands} — front, or inside.) And which two words answer it? (\emph{jī hāṅ} and \textbf{\ur{نہیں}}, from chapter one.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na … na …]{\ur{نہ} … \ur{نہ} … — neither, nor}

\label{lesson:UR-C19-na-na}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{نہیں}} stands in front of a verb. Urdu has a shorter form of the same word that stands in front of a \textbf{noun}, and it is almost always doubled.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two items before this one — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}, \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{نہ} … \ur{نہ} …}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{نہ} \ur{پانی،} \ur{نہ} \ur{ہوا}} — \emph{na pānī, na hawā} — \textbf{neither water nor air.}
\end{quote}

One \textbf{\ur{نہ}} in front of each thing refused. Strip the \textbf{-\ur{یں}} off \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} and what is left is \textbf{\ur{نہ}}, the older and shorter negator: the two are the same word at different stages of wear, which is why the doubled refusal sounds like the plain one cut short.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three negators, told apart by what follows them}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{stands before} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{نہیں}} & a verb & \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} \\
\textbf{\ur{نہیں}} & alone & the complete answer \emph{no} \\
\textbf{\ur{نہ} … \ur{نہ}} & each refused noun & \emph{na pānī, na hawā} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Urdu has a third, \emph{mat}, which belongs in front of a command — and this book has no command yet, so it waits. Its second letter has no lesson in the script ladder either, which is a second reason to leave it where it is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{na pānī, na hawā}
  \item \emph{na chāy, na dūdh} — neither tea nor milk
  \item \emph{na garmī, na sardī} — neither heat nor cold
  \item the refusal as a question — \emph{kyā pānī hai?} … \emph{nahīṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which negator stands in front of a verb, and which in front of a noun? (\textbf{\ur{نہیں}} before a verb; \textbf{\ur{نہ}} before each refused noun.) How many \textbf{\ur{نہ}} does \emph{neither … nor} need? (\textbf{Two, one for each thing}.) And what is \textbf{\ur{نہ}} to \textbf{\ur{نہیں}}? (\textbf{The same word, shorter and older}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nahīṅ · kyā · na]{Asking, and being able to say no}

\label{lesson:UR-R19-three-refusals}



\begin{quote}
Three items landed in this chapter, and between them they let the book ask a question and let you refuse it. Name all three, and say what each one stands in front of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the sentence chapter one deferred — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} a question the book can now ask — \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} both answers — \emph{jī hāṅ} … \emph{nahīṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} a double refusal — \emph{na pānī, na hawā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} a negative asked back, which is how you check something you suspect — \emph{kyā āp nahīṅ samajhte?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the reply from chapter four, then deny it — \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ} … \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk nahīṅ hūṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word turns a statement into a yes-or-no question, and where does it go? (\textbf{\ur{کیا}}, at the \textbf{front}.) Which word denies a verb, and where does it go? (\textbf{\ur{نہیں}}, \textbf{before} the verb.) And what is the shorter form of that word for? (\textbf{Refusing a noun}, doubled — \emph{na … na}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
